nameStory: This fungus doesn't have a widely-used common name, so it goes by its scientific name Climacocystis borealis. The name 'borealis' means 'northern,' telling us this is a cold-climate species that thrives in the northern forests. 'Climacocystis' refers to its ladder-like spore structure, though you'd need a microscope to see that detail.
description: Climacocystis borealis is a bracket fungus that grows as shelf-like projections from dead or dying trees. It belongs to the polypore family, meaning it has tiny pores on its underside instead of gills. These sturdy, woody brackets can persist for months or even years once formed. They're typically white to cream colored when fresh, becoming more brownish with age.

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: The underside has tiny, round pores instead of gills - look like pinpricks in a white to cream surface that may bruise yellowish when touched

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Forms thick, bracket-like shelves that are white to cream when young, becoming tan or light brown with age and weather exposure

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels firm and woody when mature, with a somewhat fuzzy or velvety surface on top that becomes smoother over time

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Grows directly from tree trunks and logs without a stem, often forming overlapping tiers of brackets

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Fresh specimens may have a faint, pleasant mushroomy smell, while older brackets become essentially odorless

habitat: Found growing on dead hardwood trees and logs throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests. Particularly common on beech, birch, and maple trees at various elevations from lowland forests to mountain slopes. Look for it in mature forests where there's plenty of fallen timber and standing dead trees.

seasonality.spring: New bracket growth may begin as small white bumps on dead trees, especially after wet spring weather creates ideal growing conditions.
seasonality.summer: Active growing season when fresh brackets expand and mature, showing their brightest white pore surfaces and most distinct features.
seasonality.fall: Brackets continue to develop and are easily spotted as leaves fall, revealing more dead wood habitat where they grow.
seasonality.winter: Persistent brackets remain visible on trees and can be found year-round, though they become darker and more weathered looking.

funFact: This northern fungus acts like nature's slow-motion recycling plant, taking years to completely break down a fallen log into rich forest soil - a single bracket can live and work for several years!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other white bracket fungi like Artist's Bracket or Turkey Tail, but Climacocystis borealis has distinctly round pores (not elongated) and lacks the colorful zones that many other brackets display.
contextualKnowledge: As a relatively uncommon species with only 72 recorded observations in New England, finding Climacocystis borealis is considered a good find by local mycologists and adds valuable data to our understanding of regional fungal diversity.
compareHints: Since it's the only species in its genus found in our region, compare it to other white polypores in the broader polypore family. Unlike the more common Trametes species, it lacks colorful zones and has perfectly round pores. It's also thicker and more substantial than the thin, papery brackets of species like Turkey Tail.
